title: Sickle cell dactylitis with hemolysis: decreased serum haptoglobin
vignette: A 1-year-old African American boy is brought to the emergency department by his parents with a 3-hour history of severe swelling and tenderness of the hands and feet. They do not know what caused the swelling and say that the boy cries when his hands or feet are touched. The patient has no history of recent illness and is up to date on all immunizations. The boy attends day care, but his parents are unsure about any sick contacts. His family history is significant for an older brother who died of pneumococcal sepsis at age 6. Physical examination shows bilateral, severe swelling of the hands and feet. Which of the following is most likely abnormal in this patient?

clues.text: severe swelling and tenderness of the hands and feet
clues.note: Painful, symmetric swelling of the hands and feet in an infant is DACTYLITIS (hand-foot syndrome) - a common early vasoocclusive manifestation of sickle cell disease.

clues.text: older brother who died of pneumococcal sepsis at age 6
clues.note: Fatal pneumococcal (encapsulated organism) sepsis in a sibling suggests FUNCTIONAL ASPLENIA - characteristic of sickle cell disease (autosplenectomy).

whatMatters: Dactylitis + family history of pneumococcal sepsis (functional asplenia) in an African American infant = SICKLE CELL DISEASE. Sickling causes chronic HEMOLYSIS, so free hemoglobin binds and consumes haptoglobin -> DECREASED serum HAPTOGLOBIN (plus increased indirect bilirubin/LDH). Answer D.
strategy: Diagnose sickle cell disease (dactylitis, autosplenectomy leading to encapsulated-organism sepsis), then pick the hemolysis marker: haptoglobin binds free hemoglobin and is CONSUMED/DECREASED in intravascular hemolysis. Reject markers of unrelated processes: LV systolic function (high-output state, usually preserved early), albumin/urine cortisol (normal in SCD), C4 complement (hereditary angioedema - autosomal dominant painless swelling, not sickle vasoocclusion), and systemic venous pressure (heart failure, not this).

eliminations.label: LV systolic function - preserved early
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: cardiac contractile function. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: chronic anemia raises cardiac output (preserved/high systolic function early); heart failure develops only later, so this isn't the abnormality in a 1-year-old with dactylitis. ✅ Correct if: chronic ischemic cardiomyopathy in older SCD patients.

eliminations.label: Serum albumin - normal in SCD
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a marker of nutrition/hepatic synthesis/protein loss. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: albumin is typically normal in sickle cell disease and dactylitis. ✅ Correct if: nephrotic syndrome/malnutrition/liver failure.

eliminations.label: C4 complement - hereditary angioedema
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a low C4 seen in hereditary angioedema (C1-inhibitor deficiency). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: hereditary angioedema causes PAINLESS episodic swelling of face/lips/larynx/extremities (autosomal dominant), not the painful vasoocclusive dactylitis of SCD. ✅ Correct if: painless angioedema with low C4 and family history (C1-inhibitor deficiency).

eliminations.label: Systemic venous pressure - heart failure
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: elevated central venous pressure (right heart failure/volume overload). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: not a feature of acute dactylitis; it reflects heart failure. ✅ Correct if: congestive heart failure/volume overload.

eliminations.label: Urine cortisol - Cushing/adrenal
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a measure of cortisol production (Cushing syndrome). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: unrelated to sickle cell disease/dactylitis. ✅ Correct if: hypercortisolism workup.

reasoning: Dactylitis + family history of pneumococcal sepsis (autosplenia) in an African American infant = sickle cell disease
Sickled cells undergo intra- and extravascular hemolysis
Hemolysis releases free hemoglobin, which binds and depletes haptoglobin
mechanism: SICKLE CELL DISEASE (homozygous HbS) is the most common autosomal recessive disorder in African Americans. Its manifestations include (1) VASOOCCLUSION: sickled cells obstruct small vessels, causing painful infarctions; in infants/young children, small infarcts of the hand and foot bones (which still contain hematopoietic marrow) cause DACTYLITIS (hand-foot syndrome) with painful, symmetric swelling; (2) INFECTIONS: repeated splenic infarcts cause FUNCTIONAL ASPLENIA/autosplenectomy, predisposing to overwhelming sepsis from ENCAPSULATED organisms (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae - explaining the sibling's death); and (3) HEMOLYSIS: repeated sickling deforms and destroys red cells (intra- and extravascular), releasing free hemoglobin. HAPTOGLOBIN binds circulating free hemoglobin, so it is CONSUMED and DECREASED (a marker of hemolysis), alongside increased INDIRECT bilirubin and LACTATE DEHYDROGENASE. Therefore serum haptoglobin is the abnormal value. The distractors relate to other conditions (hereditary angioedema for low C4, heart failure for venous pressure) or are normal in SCD (albumin, cortisol, early systolic function).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Heme > sickle cell disease: dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome) in young children; autosplenectomy -> encapsulated organism sepsis; hemolysis -> decreased haptoglobin, increased indirect bilirubin/LDH; autosomal recessive (African Americans).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Sickle cell hemolysis -> free hemoglobin binds haptoglobin -> decreased serum haptoglobin.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on dactylitis, autosplenectomy/functional asplenia, haptoglobin, hemolysis markers, or encapsulated organisms? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Low C4 = hereditary angioedema (painless swelling); albumin/cortisol/venous pressure/LV function aren't the acute SCD abnormality.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: hemolysis markers = LOW haptoglobin, HIGH indirect bilirubin + LDH; sickle cell dactylitis + autosplenia.

firstAid.detail: Heme: decreased haptoglobin (binds free Hb); increased bilirubin/LDH.
Heme > hand-foot syndrome in young children.

memoryHook: Sickled cells burst and spill hemoglobin; haptoglobin mops it up until it runs out - so a hemolyzing sickle-cell kid has LOW haptoglobin.
